summary: An overview of the Common Authentication Technology work, which aimed to give applications a common way to use authentication and related security services. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Many different locks make life hard for a keyring. This memo gives the big picture of a plan to make security checks work one way for everyone.

questions: what is the cat working group
subtitle: A framework for security services that any network protocol can use.

tldr.problem: Each network protocol implementing security had to build its own authentication mechanism, wasting effort and forcing applications to understand multiple incompatible security approaches.
tldr.mechanism: The CAT (Common Authentication Technology) working group defined the Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API), a uniform interface that any protocol can use, with Kerberos V5 and Distributed Authentication Services as underlying mechanisms.
tldr.outcome: The GSS-API became a standard way for protocols to request security services without knowing the details of the underlying authentication technology, enabling code reuse and simplifying implementations.

today: RFC 1511 outlined the CAT working group's strategy and key accomplishments. The GSS-API remains a standard approach to security integration in network protocols. Kerberos is widely deployed in enterprise environments, while other mechanisms have seen limited adoption compared to the GSS-API framework itself.

sections.title: The Problem of Scattered Security Implementations
sections.content: Before the CAT working group, each network protocol had to implement its own security mechanisms. This meant protocols could not share security code, and application developers had to understand multiple, incompatible security approaches. The CAT working group sought to separate security implementation tasks from the protocols that use them, allowing single security implementations to be reused across multiple protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Every protocol had its own way to check passwords, which was wasteful and confusing.

sections.title: The Generic Security Service Interface
sections.content: The CAT group developed the GSS-API, a mechanism-independent model for security integration. Applications call GSS-API functions to get authentication services, peer entity authentication, and optionally data origin authentication, integrity and confidentiality. The API hides the details of whether Kerberos, public-key technology, or another mechanism is being used underneath. This insulation allows protocols and applications to focus on their own functions rather than security implementation details.
sections.plainLanguage: All protocols can ask the same security service for help, without needing to know how it works inside.

sections.title: Implementations and Mechanisms
sections.content: The CAT group pursued agreements on underlying security technologies and their protocols. RFC 1510 documents Kerberos Version 5, based on secret-key cryptography and contributed by MIT. RFC 1507 documents Distributed Authentication Services (DAS), based on X.509 public-key technology and contributed by Digital Equipment Corporation. Both implement the GSS-API model, and additional mechanisms are anticipated. RFC 1508 documents the GSS-API itself, and RFC 1509 provides C-language bindings.
sections.plainLanguage: Different security methods can plug into the common interface, so people can pick which one they want.
